The house stirs. I'll take what Marta offers.

Idris Thorne takes the bread from his sister's hand. Says nothing. He's been saying nothing about markers for forty years; silence is his trade now as much as timber.

He looks at Wren. The boy has questions written all over him, the same questions Idris has watched him carry for weeks. Bram Holloway's nephew losing sleep. Nell's secret pressing against the walls of both houses.

"Aye," he says to Marta. That's the whole of his goodbye to the house.

Then he's through the door, Corwin falling in beside him, the forest waiting.

But Wren. Wren stays behind, still standing in the yard, still holding those questions. Idris could end it with one sentence. Forty years of keeping a promise he made to a woman who was young then, who thought she was settling something. Instead the young just inherit the weight.

He meets Wren's eye across the threshold. Says nothing. Walks. The trees close around him. Here, at least, a man knows what he owes the world and gives it. The axe speaks plain. The timber falls where he reads it will fall. No promises buried in the roots, no markers moved by hands that are dust now.

He sets to work.  Two trees down before the sun climbs. The work costs, but the wood warms both houses through the winter. His household. The Holloways. Forty years of cutting wood that crosses the same disputed line.

He does not look at the boundary. He never does.

The axe bites. Timber falls. Two trees down, and Idris pauses to let the forest settle around the new silence he's made.

He sets another tree. Reads the grain, the lean, the weight of branches. A beech this time, not yet full grown but straight enough for beams. His eye finds the fall line before he swings. The work is what he trusts—where a tree will land, how the weight will shift, what the ground will bear.

Corwin works fifty paces off. His nephew by marriage, closer to him than blood would make some. The boy asks careful questions about felling, about seasoning, about which wood takes the plane clean. Idris answers in his way: a gesture, a corrected grip on the axe, a glance at the wrong angle that says *not there*.

They work until the light changes. Then Idris carries what he's cut downslope, where the cart road begins. Corwin follows with his own load.

The day earns what it needs to. Timber stacked for seasoning, some bound for the mill at week's end. The forest gives and takes. The boundary he does not look at stands somewhere behind them, marked by a stone moved forty years ago by a woman who wanted peace and built instead a silence that outlived her reasons.

He does not think about telling Wren. He does not think about telling anyone. A promise outlasts. That is the whole of it.

He shoulders his pack and walks home through the trees.

I don't need a plan. The forest tells me what's next. 

Idris works another hour. Two more trees—oak, this time, the dense wood that burns slow through winter. He reads each one before he swings. The grain, the lean, whether the ground will hold the fall or send it wide. He has not been wrong in thirty years of cutting.

Corwin works steady nearby. The boy has questions he does not ask. Idris can hear them anyway, in the pause between strokes, in the way he sets his feet.

They speak little. The work speaks.

By the time the sun clears the ridge, they have timber enough for a quarter season. Idris binds his load, counts what he'll bring to market, what he'll stack for the households. Both houses. Always both. The wood crosses boundaries. The work does not care whose marker said what.

He shoulders his pack. Walks the cart road home. Corwin falls in beside him, matching his pace.

The Holloway question waits in the town below. Wren's sleeplessness. Bram's stubbornness. Nell's forty-year silence that Idris keeps like another tree to fell, another load to carry.

He does not speak of it. He will not speak of it.

They walk down through the trees, toward the houses, toward whatever the day brings.
